2.1.3 Extending Risk Assessments Through Vulnerability Scans

Risks should be validated through vulnerability scans. These, also sometimes called pentesting,

detect weaknesses in the system by scanning for missing updates, patches,6 or existing

misconfigurations. Vulnerability scans should be conducted at planned intervals (for example,

annually) and when significant changes to port systems occur. They should be accompanied by an

updated risk register, which is a prioritized inventory of the most significant risks to achieving the

set objectives. It is maintained to track ownership and due dates for risk mitigation actions and to

monitor any changes to risk levels. Examples of risk mitigation actions, as well as further technical

resources for the reader, are provided in Appendix 3: Further Resources to Improve Protection.

foundation for developing an evidence-based understanding of cyber risk in ports.

Effective cyber risk management favors a continuous, proactive approach. This means anticipating

threats, improving controls, monitoring digital signals, and making changes on a continuous basis,

rather than waiting to react after incidents occur, as illustrated in Figure 6 below. This shift reduces

cyber exposure and incident response time by embedding prevention, detection, and response into daily

operations, whereas a reactive model largely focuses on post-incident containment and recovery.

2. Practice: Develop and maintain an up-to-date inventory of physical and IT assets and identify

critical assets needed for the continuous operation of the port ecosystem. Continuously

assess cyber risk exposure, implement risk mitigation measures and business continuity plans,

and clearly define responsibilities. These plans should be validated with internal or external

tests and exercise drills, and resources should be focused on the most critical systems, key

providers, and sensitive data, to maintain or rapidly recover port operations. Modernize legacy

technologies, leverage advanced technologies such as AI-based tools to enhance resilience,

and assess emerging technologies for cyber risks early in the adoption lifecycle. Organizations

are encouraged to move from a reactive, incident-driven approach to cybersecurity toward a

proactive, continuous management system.

3.2 Financial Barriers

Even where ports recognize the skills gap discussed above, they frequently cannot justify

the investment — not because they are indifferent to risk, but because the financial logic of

cybersecurity works against them. Among World Bank survey respondents, funding cybersecurity

is an important barrier for more than 50 percent of ports across all income groups. The lack of a

business case is also widely recognized as a core barrier among ports. Unlike the human capacity

barriers discussed above, financial barriers concern what ports are willing to spend. This is distinct

from the market failures discussed in Section 3.3, which persist even where the financial case

becomes clear and adequate investments are present.

Security in general and cybersecurity in particular do not provide direct revenue to an organization

results.source: Cybersecurity in Ports - Shifting from Risk to Resilience.pdf
results.text:
accompanied by broad awareness programs for ports workforce. Financial barriers include funding

pressures and the perceived absence of a compelling business case. These factors reduce investment

in cybersecurity controls, as such measures avert losses rather than produce measurable revenue.

Economic barriers arise when different parties do not share the same goals and problems spill over:

if one operator cuts back on cybersecurity, it can raise risks for everyone else, creating so-called

negative externalities. Some parties may be tempted to benefit from others’ investments without

contributing themselves, free-riding8 on others (Moore 2010). On top of that, information gaps make

it hard to assess risks clearly and learn from past events. This chapter examines these key barriers

to improving cybersecurity in ports and first discusses human capacity barriers (3.1), then financial

barriers (3.2), and finally economic barriers (3.3).

Selected recommendations:

• Training: Implement role-based, recurrent cybersecurity training across all staff levels, covering

both IT and OT threat scenarios.

• Culture: Foster a no-blame reporting culture that treats incident disclosure as a contribution to

collective defense rather than an admission of failure.

• Incentives: Treat cyber-resilient supply chains as a public good and reflect this in governance

frameworks and contractual arrangements. For example, invest in cyber resilience centers

and cross-sector capacity building to enhance coordinated detection, intelligence sharing, and

incident response capabilities.
